title: Absolute moment of a Gaussian linear functional
statement:
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer, let $\gamma_n$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$, and let $L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous linear functional. If $e_i$ are the standard coordinate vectors, then
\[\int |L(z)|\,d\gamma_n(z)=\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n L(e_i)^2}\,2\varphi(0),\]
where $\varphi$ is the standard Gaussian density on $\mathbb R$.
hypotheses_covered: $L$ is a continuous linear functional from $\mathbb R^n$ to $\mathbb R$
replaced: Let $\gamma_n$ be standard Gaussian measure on $\mathbb R^n$ and $X,Y$ independent with that law. For a linear functional $L:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$, put $|L|_2=\sqrt{\sum_i L(e_i)^2}$, where $e_i$ is the canonical basis. Then $\mathbb E|L(X)|=|L|_2\,2\varphi(0)$, where $\varphi$ is the one-dimensional standard Gaussian density.
